title: Knight VS 2 Rooks
summary: Use queen checks to arrange the rooks as blockers, then sacrifice the queen for a knight mate.

nodes.question: How can White rearrange a strong defensive shelter?
nodes.explanation: After Qa1+ and ...Rd1, Black’s king sits behind two rooks and a knight. White can use checks to control where those defenders stand.

nodes.question: Does a checking interposition stop the attack?
nodes.explanation: Qe3+ forces Black to block on e2. The two possible blockers lead to the same Nf3 mating idea.

branches.title: Meet a checking knight block with a queen sacrifice
commentary: Begin after Qa1+ ...Rd1 in the stable seven-piece board. Earlier Qa4+ and the king escape remain source context.
Qc3+ changes the checking diagonal to c3–d2–e1. The automatic captions incorrectly call this Qc4; the stable saved diagrams show c3.
Rdd2 interposes with the rook from d1, preserving the apparent shelter while blocking the diagonal check.
Qc1+ checks along the first rank, forcing Black to change the rook’s square again.
Rd1 blocks the check and leaves d2 free for the queen’s diagonal route.
Qe3+ checks along the e-file, placing Black under a new interposition problem.
Ne2+ blocks with check against Kg1. Black hopes the checking tempo will force White to abandon the attack.
Qxe2+ answers the check by capturing the blocking knight and sacrificing the queen with check.
Rxe2 accepts with the rook from f2. The black rooks now occupy d1 and e2, boxing in their own king.
Nf3# gives actual mate. Nf3 checks Ke1 and covers d2; Kg1 covers f1 and f2, while the black rooks occupy d1 and e2.
branches.explanation: Nf3# gives actual mate. Nf3 checks Ke1 and covers d2; Kg1 covers f1 and f2, while the black rooks occupy d1 and e2.

branches.title: Block with the rook instead
commentary: Compare the source’s other legal interposition after Qe3+.
Re2 blocks the queen’s check with the rook from f2, leaving Black’s own king boxed behind Rd1 and Re2.
Nf3# gives actual mate immediately. The queen need not be sacrificed because the black knight has not arrived on e2 to force a capture.
branches.explanation: Nf3# gives actual mate immediately. The queen need not be sacrificed because the black knight has not arrived on e2 to force a capture.

exercises.prompt: Why check on c1 before going to e3?
exercises.answer: Qc1+ draws the rook back to d1, clearing d2 so the queen can travel from c1 through d2 to e3.

exercises.prompt: Why does Qxe2+ work while White is in check?
exercises.answer: It captures the checking knight, answers the check, and gives check itself. The forced rook recapture places both black rooks on the king’s escape squares before Nf3 mate.

startContext: Begin after Qa1+ ...Rd1 at 27 seconds in a stable complete seven-piece board. The queen route Qc3+, Qc1+ and Qe3+ is reconstructed from saved images; repeated source resets are not encoded as consecutive moves. Both interpositions on e2 lead to checked actual mates.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.

sourceCorrections.claim: Automatic captions describe the queen withdrawal as Qc4 and omit the repeated Qc1+ rook interposition.
sourceCorrections.correction: Stable boards show Qc3 ...Rd2 Qc1+ ...Rd1 before Qe3+. Qa1–c4 is not a legal queen move; going directly from c1 to e3 while Rd2 remains would also be blocked. The encoded sequence follows the saved board states.
